summary: The focus of our project is to study storms on Mars, which, in turn, complicate humanity's efforts toward further colonization. This presentation will offer suggestions on how to solve this problem.
details:
Today, Mars exploration is shifting from isolated reconnaissance probes to
the design of permanent scientific bases and crewed expeditions. The main natural
threat to equipment or crew there is large-scale dust storms. A dense curtain
of microscopic dust obscures the sky, and sunlight barely reaches the
surface, leading to a rapid drop in battery charge, disruption of the thermal
balance of instruments, loss of visibility, and radio communication failures.
The most famous example of this danger was the global dust storm of 2018, which
led to the loss of NASA’s Opportunity rover on Meridiani (Meridiani
Planum). This event demonstrated that missions need user-friendly interactive maps that allow for
the assessment of dust risks in advance, the planning of alternate routes, and the placement of
life-support facilities.
To address this challenge, we developed the interactive, multi-layered
GIS map “MARS: STORM ALERT” using Opportunity’s historical operating area
in the Meridiani Planum region as a case study. The project’s core concept involves combining real
NASA satellite data with simulated elements of a future
expedition. We implemented the map as a lightweight web console that opens in
a standard browser without the need for complex specialized software.
For the scientific basis, we used open-access NASA satellite data for
the Meridiani Planum sector centered at coordinates 1.95° south latitude and 354.47°
east longitude. The MOLA raster layer—data
from the Mars Global Surveyor’s laser altimeter—is responsible for rendering the terrain. To recreate weather conditions,
we turned to the MARCI camera archive from the Mars Reconnaissance
Orbiter. A real-time sequence of MARCI images from May 31 through June 11, 2018,
served as the basis for our twelve-stage timeline: it shows how the storm on June 2
reached Opportunity’s operating area and subsequently expanded to a planetary
scale.
Technically, the “MARS: STORM ALERT” dashboard combines eleven thematic layers
of data: the MOLA topographic map, a coordinate grid, dust hazard layers divided
into three risk zones, temperature context, travel routes, scientific sites,
and survival sites. Users can turn individual layers on or off, view
object information cards, as well as place their own markers on the map and save notes in
a JSON file.
On the map, we have modeled a research expedition within a fifty-kilometer radius
around Opportunity’s landing site. We have placed the crew’s main living quarters, the solar
panel array, water tanks, and oxygen storage facility in the southwest—in
the sector with the lowest dust risk level. Scientific research sites are concentrated in the north and northeast,
and the autonomous
emergency shelter, Shelter E, is located on the eastern edge of the map. A main route for calm
weather and two alternative evacuation routes in case of danger have been laid out between the facilities.
Under normal conditions, the crew works unhindered at remote scientific
research sites. But as soon as we switch to dust storm mode or move the time slider
forward, the dust cloud expands to the southeast, triggering a high-risk red zone
high-risk zone, and backup escape routes automatically appear: the group from
the northern sector urgently returns to the main base, while the team from the central
sector moves eastward to Shelter E. At the same time, the map interface clearly
distinguishes between real NASA scientific observations and simulated elements of the
training simulation.
In the future, this prototype can be transformed into a precise engineering tool by
integrating data from the MCS (Mars Climate Sounder) instrument and ultra-high-resolution orbital images from
the THEMIS and HiRISE cameras. Already today, the “MARS: STORM ALERT” console serves as
a convenient browser-based simulator for training, command exercises, and the analysis of
space threats.
dataRefs: The Martian Dust Storm of June 2018
